content: The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) recommend a comprehensive package of nine interventions to prevent, treat, and manage HIV among people who inject drugs. These interventions include needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy, HIV testing and counseling, antiretroviral therapy (ART), prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, condom distribution programs, targeted behavior change communication, prevention and treatment of viral hepatitis, and prevention and treatment of tuberculosis (TB). WHO, UNODC, and UNAIDS have also developed technical guidance to help countries set targets for universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, and care for people who inject drugs. This includes guidelines for psychosocially assisted pharmacological treatment of opioid dependence and specific recommendations for preventing viral hepatitis B and C among people who inject drugs. For adolescents and adults living with HIV, low energy intake combined with increased energy demands due to HIV infection and related conditions can lead to weight loss and wasting. Altered metabolism, reduced appetite, and higher rates of diarrhea can further reduce nutrient intake and absorption, compounding the problem, especially in low-income and food-insecure settings. Weight loss, low body mass index (BMI), and wasting are independent risk factors for HIV disease progression and mortality. Nutritional assessment, counseling, and support should be integral to HIV care, starting at enrollment and continuing throughout treatment. Malnourished patients may require food supplements in addition to ART to support nutritional recovery. Any weight loss or failure to maintain a healthy weight during HIV infection or ART should prompt further assessment and intervention. WHO is revising its recommendations for nutritional care and support for adolescents and adults living with HIV, including pregnant and lactating women. For children living with HIV, early nutritional assessment is critical to identify malnutrition and growth faltering. Infants and children should undergo initial nutritional evaluation and be weighed and measured at each visit, with growth monitored against WHO or national growth curves. Poor growth should trigger further assessment to determine the cause and plan appropriate responses. WHO’s 2009 guidelines provide detailed recommendations for the nutritional care of children living with HIV. BMI is a key indicator of weight adequacy in relation to height for older children, adolescents, and adults. It is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. For children, BMI varies with age and should be interpreted accordingly. Palliative care, including symptom management and end-of-life care, is essential throughout all stages of HIV disease. Pain and discomfort should be addressed by identifying and treating underlying causes while managing symptoms effectively. Managing ART side effects is also critical to support adherence. Family planning, counseling, and contraception are important components of HIV care. WHO provides additional guidance on medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use and the interaction between hormonal contraception and HIV. The delivery of antiretroviral drugs and related services must be optimized to ensure effectiveness, equity, and efficiency. This includes linking care settings, supporting adherence to lifelong treatment, and retaining patients across the continuum of care. Key operational areas include adherence to ART, retention in care, service integration, decentralization of HIV care, task shifting, laboratory and diagnostic services, and procurement and supply management systems. New recommendations include using text messages to promote adherence, integrating ART with maternal and child health services, decentralizing ART delivery, and task shifting. Adherence to ART is critical for suppressing viral replication, improving clinical outcomes, reducing the risk of drug resistance, and preventing HIV transmission. Barriers to adherence include individual factors (e.g., forgetting doses, depression, substance use), medication-related factors (e.g., side effects, complex regimens), and health system factors (e.g., frequent clinic visits, long travel distances). Supportive environments and addressing stigma and discrimination are essential for improving adherence. Pregnant and postpartum women face unique challenges to adherence, including pregnancy-related conditions like nausea, concerns about ART’s effects on the fetus, and fear of disclosing HIV status. Adolescents also face barriers such as stigma, peer pressure, and transitioning from pediatric to adult care. For children, adherence is complicated by limited pediatric formulations, poor palatability, and the need for caregiver involvement. Mental health disorders, such as depression, can negatively impact adherence to ART. Addressing mental health comorbidities through counseling and medical therapies can improve adherence and treatment outcomes. Similarly, substance use disorders can interfere with adherence due to forgetfulness, poor organization, and competing priorities. Interventions to optimize adherence to ART should be tailored to individual needs and barriers. Program-level strategies include avoiding out-of-pocket payments, using fixed-dose combination regimens, and strengthening drug supply systems. Individual-level interventions, such as mobile phone text messaging, should be part of a comprehensive adherence support package. Nutritional support, peer support, and management of mental health and substance use disorders are also critical components of HIV care. Efforts to support adherence should begin before ART initiation, with patient education covering basic information about HIV, ART, expected side effects, and adherence preparation. Education and counseling should continue throughout treatment, with peer support playing a significant role in improving adherence and retention. For people living with HIV who use drugs, services such as needle and syringe programs, drug dependence treatment, and peer outreach provide opportunities to support adherence and improve outcomes. Structured treatment programs within prison settings can also achieve excellent results despite the challenges of incarceration.
